evidence.section_title: Impulsivity During Times of Distress
evidence.quote: Of the 44 patients in the chart review, 34 (77%) were characterized as "impulsive." Based on partial information from the narratives of the interviews, the circumstances of the participants' suicide attempts also indicated a high level of impulsivity. Most attempts appeared to be triggered by arguments with significant others or disappointing news related to finances, housing, and employment. All the interviewees made one or more attempts in front of other people or sought help after the attempts. Various methods of suicide were reported in both samples: ingestion of prescription drugs and painkillers, wrist cutting and stabbing of body parts, hanging, and jumping into subway tracks, rivers, or from heights. Different kinds of injury ranging from minimal (superficial cuts) to potential lethality (near-death experiences, loss of speech, and gastrointestinal damage) were incurred. However, there was no pattern of increasing lethality between the various attempts, which could be another indication of the participants' impulsivity.

evidence.section_title: Life Stressors and Coping Mechanism
evidence.quote: The relatively high percentage of persons repeating attempts (34%; 10 of 29 cases) who lived alone or in shelters was in congruence with the data of social isolation noted in the overall demographic profile of the two study samples, and should still be considered as a potential indicator of the type of social instability associated with greater risk. The considerable number of common life stressors experienced by both groups suggests that a key aspect of risk resides with an individual's capability to deal effectively with adversities, as well as psychological resilience in the face of challenging life stressors.

evidence.section_title: A Mixed-Method Study of Risk and Protective Factors
evidence.quote: The study samples shared major suicide risk  factors identified in studies of other populations. Participants of the interview sample suffered from a pervasive sense of hopelessness stemming  from social isolation, self-stigma, feelings of failure in their life roles, and perceptions of rejection by their families. Conversely, psychological  well-being – feeling cared for and able to reciprocate care for others – appeared to be a protective factor for participants who improved in their  functioning and recovery.

evidence.section_title: Thematic Analysis
evidence.quote: Extensive reviews of the interview transcripts were made to organize clusters of text by themes and subthemes under the broad categories of mental illness, negative life events, past and current relationships with significant others, suicidal thoughts and behaviors, and past and current level of functioning.

evidence.section_title: Protective Factors
evidence.quote: Analysis of the interviews indicated that the strongest protective factors were linked to existential issues whereby the  participants felt a sense of purpose and competence in their  life roles. In the comparative analysis between the repeated attempters and nonattempters (Table 2), there was no  significant difference in the report of having responsibilities for children and religious practice, two variables that  are commonly perceived as suicide protective factors. In  the interview sample, these variables as protective factors  were tenuous when the participants were decompensating  from their mental illness. Among the five female participants who had children, there was a deep sense of guilt  and shame that they could not care for them, and that their  children would be better off with their extended family.  One participant believed that killing herself was a suitable  option to provide for her son who was a beneficiary of her  life insurance policy. Of the two participants who were practicing the Christian faith at the time of their suicide attempts, they heard  voices reprimanding them for their sins and urging them  to kill themselves. However, the role of these variables  as protective factors strengthened when the same participants experienced a sense of psychological well-being and  found more comfort in their faith. A comparative analysis on the protective role of existential issues was also made between six participants in  the interview sample who showed some reported improvement in their clinical symptoms and treatment adherence  and the other participants who did not make any progress  in their recovery. It appeared that these participants' recovery progress was closely related to a more positive outlook  about their lives that was missing among the other participants. There were two interrelated themes that spoke to  this glimmer of hope and optimism as well as motivation  to remain in treatment among the six participants.

evidence.section_title: A Sense of Competence in Their Life Roles
evidence.quote: In reviewing recent changes in their lives, these participants were able to articulate a sense of purpose and a vision of their future where they would be able to provide care for others, for example, infirmed or young family members, or the anticipation of a more financially stable life that would support their children in their home countries. While these changes in circumstances might not be deemed as significant improvement in the participants' quality of life, they certainly seemed to have fueled a sense of empowerment among the participants as they realized they could assume the role of reciprocating care in the family, a universal human need that was also amplified by the emphasis of interdependence in the Asian collectivistic cultures. A female participant who used to think that she should die when her parents pass away talked about why she had a change of heart: 'I don't have a lot of expectations for my life right now, but I realize that my younger brother may be dying (of cancer), and I need to take care of him and my parents.' A female participant talked with a sense of pride about how she took care of her family since her condition stabilized: 'My husband knows how to cook, but he wants me to do all the cooking. I also tidy the place every day so we can spend some family time together after dinner.'
